mcqs.question: Which of the following statements most accurately compares coalition governments with single‑party governments in India?

options.A: Coalition governments are formed only when a single party wins more than 50% of seats, whereas single‑party governments arise when no party reaches that threshold.
options.B: In coalition governments, two or more parties combine to command a majority in the legislature, while single‑party governments are formed when one party alone secures a majority.
options.C: Coalition governments always lead to stable, long‑lasting administrations, whereas single‑party governments are inherently unstable.
options.D: Coalition governments require the President’s approval, while single‑party governments are appointed solely by the Prime Minister.

mcqs.answer: In coalition governments, two or more parties combine to command a majority in the legislature, while single‑party governments are formed when one party alone secures a majority.
mcqs.explanation: In the Indian parliamentary system, if no single party wins a majority of seats, parties negotiate to form a coalition that together holds a majority. A single‑party government occurs when one party wins enough seats to govern alone. Options A, C and D contain factual errors about the conditions and stability of coalition versus single‑party governments.

mcqs.question: Which of the following pairs correctly identifies a national party and a regional party as defined in the NCERT textbook?

options.A: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) – national; Shiv Sena – regional
options.B: Indian National Congress (INC) – regional; Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) – national
options.C: Communist Party of India (CPI) – national; All India Trinamool Congress (AITC) – national
options.D: Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) – regional; Samajwadi Party (SP) – regional

mcqs.answer: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) – national; Shiv Sena – regional
mcqs.explanation: According to the NCERT criteria, the BJP meets the requirements for a national party, while Shiv Sena is recognised as a regional party limited to Maharashtra. Options B, C and D misclassify at least one of the parties, making them incorrect.

mcqs.question: What best describes a one‑party system in a democratic context?

options.A: Multiple parties compete, but only one is allowed to form the government.
options.B: Only one political party is legally permitted to exist and contest elections.
options.C: Several parties exist, but they always form a coalition to govern.
options.D: One party dominates elections, though other parties are also present.

mcqs.answer: Only one political party is legally permitted to exist and contest elections.
mcqs.explanation: A one‑party system allows only a single party to be legally recognised and to contest elections; opposition parties are banned. Option A describes a dominant‑party scenario, C describes a coalition‑prone system, and D describes a dominant‑party but not a one‑party system.

mcqs.question: In a two‑party system, which of the following statements is true?

options.A: Two parties share power equally in every election.
options.B: Only two parties are legally allowed to register with the Election Commission.
options.C: Two major parties dominate the political arena, while smaller parties have minimal influence.
options.D: The two parties always form a coalition government.

mcqs.answer: Two major parties dominate the political arena, while smaller parties have minimal influence.
mcqs.explanation: A two‑party system is characterised by the dominance of two large parties; smaller parties may exist but rarely win significant seats. Options A and D are inaccurate because power sharing and coalition are not guaranteed. Option B is false because legal registration is not limited to two parties.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly defines a multi‑party system and distinguishes it from a one‑party system?

options.A: A multi‑party system allows several parties to contest elections, but only one party can ever win a majority; a one‑party system permits only one party to exist.
options.B: In a multi‑party system, many parties compete and no single party is guaranteed a majority, often leading to coalition governments; a one‑party system has only one legal party that controls the legislature.
options.C: A multi‑party system requires parties to merge before elections; a one‑party system bans all opposition.
options.D: Multi‑party systems are found only in federal countries; one‑party systems exist only in unitary states.

mcqs.answer: In a multi‑party system, many parties compete and no single party is guaranteed a majority, often leading to coalition governments; a one‑party system has only one legal party that controls the legislature.
mcqs.explanation: The defining feature of a multi‑party system is the presence of several competitive parties, making majority governments uncertain and coalition‑building common. A one‑party system, by contrast, legally restricts politics to a single party. Options A, C and D contain incorrect or irrelevant statements.

mcqs.question: In a state election, Party X wins 40% of the seats, Party Y 35%, and Party Z 25%. No party has a majority. Which of the following actions best reflects the formation of a coalition government?

options.A: Party X forms the government alone, ignoring the shortfall.
options.B: Party Y and Party Z combine to form a coalition with a combined 60% of seats, and their leader becomes Chief Minister.
options.C: The Governor appoints a technocrat to run the state.
options.D: All three parties agree to a power‑sharing arrangement where each gets equal ministerial posts regardless of seat share.

mcqs.answer: Party Y and Party Z combine to form a coalition with a combined 60% of seats, and their leader becomes Chief Minister.
mcqs.explanation: A coalition government is created when two or more parties join forces to command a legislative majority. Option B shows exactly that. Option A ignores the need for a majority, C bypasses democratic process, and D is unrealistic because ministerial allocation usually reflects seat share, not equal division.

mcqs.question: Which of the following examples correctly matches a national party with a regional party as defined in the NCERT textbook?

options.A: National: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP); Regional: Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK)
options.B: National: Indian National Congress (INC); Regional: Nationalist Congress Party (NCP)
options.C: National: Communist Party of India (CPI); Regional: All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK)
options.D: National: Samajwadi Party (SP); Regional: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)

mcqs.answer: National: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP); Regional: Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK)
mcqs.explanation: The BJP satisfies the NCERT criteria for a national party, while the DMK operates primarily in Tamil Nadu and is classified as a regional party. In option B, NCP is also a national party, making the pairing wrong. Option C mislabels CPI, which is not a national party under the textbook criteria. Option D reverses the classifications.

mcqs.question: In the fictional country of Lankara, the same party has won every election since independence, and opposition parties are banned. Which political system does this scenario illustrate?
mcqs.explanation: A one‑party system is characterised by the existence of only one legal political party, with all opposition parties prohibited. The description of Lankara matches this definition. Options A, B and D involve multiple parties, which contradict the scenario.
